one_liner: Go proto3 RPC generator that swaps gRPC's HTTP/2 and Protobuf for 8-byte-header TCP framing and Polyglot encoding.
what_it_does: fRPC is a protoc plugin (protoc-gen-go-frpc) that turns existing proto3 files into Go message structs, a Server and a Client. The generated server interfaces use grpc-go's signatures (Method(ctx, *Req) (*Res, error)), so a gRPC handler implementation can be reused. It also generates unary and client, server and bidirectional streaming RPCs; streaming landed in 2022, although the docs overview still lists it as unsupported. The wire protocol is not gRPC, so both ends must be fRPC. One generated Client covers every service, and you can drop to the underlying frisbee connection or take the raw net.Conn back for another protocol.
how_it_is_fast: HTTP/2 framing is replaced by Frisbee's fixed 8-byte packet header (uint16 request id, uint16 operation, uint32 length) on a plain TCP or TLS net.Conn. Protobuf is replaced by Polyglot, which writes fields positionally with typed encode calls and no field tags. Packets and header buffers come from pools, and the unary server handler reuses the incoming packet as the response buffer. Writes go into a 64 KiB bufio.Writer that a separate flush goroutine drains, so many small RPCs are coalesced into fewer syscalls; the headline numbers also used the mode that runs handlers inline on each connection's goroutine instead of spawning one per RPC.
when_to_use: Go-to-Go services you own on both ends, on a trusted network, where you want proto3 schemas without HTTP/2 and Protobuf overhead.
Many small, non-blocking unary RPCs per connection (echo, metrics, telemetry), where the single-goroutine-per-connection mode applies.
Thousands of concurrent client connections to one server; this is where the project's benchmark shows grpc-go's per-client throughput falling off hardest (112 vs 29 RPC/s per client at 8192 clients).
Protocols that mix request/reply with custom Frisbee messaging patterns (e.g. pub/sub) or hand the TCP connection to something else after the RPCs.
when_not_to_use: Any non-Go peer, browser, gRPC tooling (grpcurl, reflection) or gRPC-aware proxy or mesh: the wire format is Frisbee plus Polyglot, and the roadmap still lists JS/TS, Rust and WebSocket support as planned.

Rolling deploys where client and server run different schema versions: Polyglot encodes fields in declaration order with no tags, and the maintainers confirmed on HN (2022) that it lacks protobuf's forward/backward compatibility.

When you rely on gRPC features: there is no built-in load balancing or retries (per the roadmap), no status codes (errors go over the wire as Polyglot error values), no interceptor/metadata API, and no deadline propagation (ctx cancellation only stops the client waiting).
Untrusted or internet-facing peers: the 32-bit length field is honored with no max-message-size check, so the read buffer grows to whatever size the peer declares.
Anything needing an active upstream: the README calls it early Alpha, the last code change was November 2024, and later commits are only dependency bumps.

integration.dependencies: Build time: protoc (proto3) and the protoc-gen-go-frpc plugin. Runtime (go.mod): github.com/loopholelabs/frisbee-go v0.10.2, github.com/loopholelabs/polyglot/v2, github.com/loopholelabs/logging.
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.22 (go.mod and README badge; the docs site still says 1.18+)
integration.platforms: Any platform Go supports, over any net.Conn transport; no OS- or CPU-specific code found
integration.thread_safety: Generated client methods can be called concurrently: the id counter and in-flight map are mutex-guarded. Frisbee's SetConcurrency doc says server handlers must be thread-safe when they share state across connections, and also per connection unless concurrency is 1.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — server handler signatures match grpc-go, so service code ports with little change; client/server construction differs (NewServer(svc..., *tls.Config, logger), a single NewClient), the wire protocol is not gRPC so every peer must switch, and oneof, interceptors, status codes, load balancing and retries are missing

gotchas: The published numbers used SetConcurrency(1) (the benchmark server sets it unless sleeping), not the default of one goroutine per RPC. In that mode handlers run inline on the connection's read goroutine, so one slow handler stalls every RPC on that connection.
oneof is not rejected: the generator flattens it into ordinary struct fields and encodes all of them, with no 'which field is set' semantics. The README lists OneOf as unsupported.
Unary request ids are uint16, per method, per client, and wrap around. More than 65,535 concurrent in-flight calls to one method on one client can collide in the in-flight map.

Frisbee applies a fixed 5 s deadline (DefaultDeadline) to every socket read and write and sends a PING every 500 ms (DefaultPingInterval), and the generated fRPC API exposes neither. A write that cannot complete within 5 s closes the connection.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick fRPC over rpcx or cmd-stream when you want to keep proto3 files and grpc-go-shaped handler signatures while generating Go-only code. Its claimed gap over grpc-go (roughly 2-4x) is in the same band as rpcx (2.3-2.6x) and cmd-stream (3.2-4.6x), so let its alpha status and stale maintenance, not the numbers, decide.
verified_claims_summary: These are first-party results from August 2022 code: fRPC on frisbee-go v0.6.0 against grpc-go v1.48.0 with a default grpc.NewServer(), a single-string-field echo proto, go.mod 'go 1.18', and the actual Go toolchain and flags not stated, on a bare-metal Debian 11 host with 2x AMD EPYC 7643 and 256 GB RAM over a local network. fRPC reached 112 vs 29 RPC/s per client at 32 B and 98 vs 29 at 512 B (8192 clients), 192 vs 65 at 128 KB (100 clients), and about 3.6 vs 1.7 GB/s at 1 MB (about 2.1x, although the page says 3-4x); server throughput was over 2M vs just under 500k RPC/s, and about 1.6M vs 400k with a 50 us sleep in the default goroutine-per-RPC mode.
status_note: Stale: the last commit was 2025-09-22 (dependency bumps), the last release v0.10.2 on 2024-11-07, Dependabot PRs including a frisbee-go 0.11.0 bump sit unmerged, and the benchmark repo was archived on 2026-07-21. It is Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor (Go templates plus a generator), but you also inherit frisbee-go and polyglot.
